Did you know that you are not limited just by the size of your kiln when making large ceramics! The best way to build big pottery in my opinion his with coils. I’m making a floor lamp for a client and decided that stacking multiple pieces was how I was going to get the hight required for a piece of clay furniture! I love how that pottery really is just using the same dozen or so techniques in a bunch of different combinations, and that your creativity can allow you to really break through what is “possible”. lidded jar tutorial - part 1 (throwing the jar body and lid)✨ have to break this up into 3 parts because it will take weeks to go through the steps (we're making these jars in real time and rely on a community studio to fire) and I simply can't fit throwing, trimming, and glazing the jars into one reel 🥲 i find 200g is perfect for throwing the small jar body, plus another 150g for the lid. you'll see i throw my jar body and lid separately, leaving a lot of the refining for the trimming stage. especially with the lids, I find it easier to throw them roughly and finesse the fit once they're leather hard. i don't wire off the lids or jars, i wait until they pop off the bats. xo shan #pottery #potterytutorial #liddedjar #handmadeceramics #canadianartist

Here’s a completed apothecary jar and a full overview of how it’s made. For this type of lidded jar, the base and lid are thrown from one continuous piece of clay, then cut open and trimmed to create the inner edges and gallery so the lid doesn’t slide off. I like this type of piece because it has a continuous line from the base to the top of the knob. It’s a very elegant shape and one I imagine would look lovely on a shelf holding trinkets, spices, or chocolates. #pottery #studioceramics #wheelthrown #handmade #potteryartist

Throwing a Donut on the Wheel Center your clay and compress it into a wide, flat puck. Poke through the center down to the wheel head and slowly stretch it open to create the donut hole. Split the ring 50/50—leave a base slightly thicker than your future walls. Pull up the inner wall first, then the outer wall. Join the walls together. It doesn’t matter which one overlaps—adjust based on how the clay moves. Before joining, I thin out the edges to avoid a step at the seam. Important! Remove any slip and excess water from the seam—otherwise, it will crack during drying or firing. Once the walls are joined, the trapped air inside acts as a support structure, allowing you to refine the shape and compress the seam. Trim the excess clay inside and out, and your donut is ready!
